L12@P0: Abstract— This paper treats the subject of fundamental
L13@P0: guidance principles related to motion behaviour in a 2D plane
L14@P0: and a 3D space. In this context, the concept of guidance-based
L15@P0: path following is defined and elaborated upon. Its specifics
L16@P0: are contrasted towards the already established concept of
L17@P0: trajectory tracking. Specifically, guidance laws are developed
L18@P0: at an ideal, dynamics-independent level to yield generally valid
L19@P0: laws uninfluenced by the particularities of any specific dynamics
L20@P0: case. These laws can subsequently be tailored to actual target
L21@P0: systems like e.g. watercraft or spacecraft, for instance in
L22@P0: a cascaded setting. The approach renders all regular paths
L23@P0: feasible. Possible applications and extensions to the guidancebased path following scheme are also briefly suggested.
L24@P0: I. INTRODUCTION
L25@P0: The ability to maneuver an actual target system like a
L26@P0: watercraft or a spacecraft accurately along a desired geometric path is a primary objective for most applications.
L27@P0: An objective like satisfying some desired dynamic behaviour
L28@P0: while traversing the path would consequently be viewed upon
L29@P0: as secondary. If given the freedom to construct a desired
L30@P0: geometric path for an actual system to converge to and
L31@P0: follow, the choice of a solution strategy to fulfill the task
L32@P0: at hand would traditionally stand between the concepts of
L33@P0: trajectory tracking (TT) and path following (PF).
L34@P0: To illustrate the difference between these two schemes,
L35@P0: we will employ the notion of an actual particle and a path
L36@P0: particle. An actual particle is a position variable belonging
L37@P0: to an actual system. It represents the position variable whose
L38@P0: goal is to converge to and follow the desired geometric path.
L39@P0: A path particle, on the other hand, is a position variable
L40@P0: belonging to the desired geometric path, restricted to move
L41@P0: along it at all times.
L42@P0: The TT scheme entails the simultaneous construction of
L43@P0: the geometric path and the dynamic behaviour of the path
L44@P0: particle. Hence, it inherently mixes the space and time
L45@P0: assignments into one single assignment, demanding that any
L46@P0: actual target system is located at a specific point in space at
L47@P0: a specific, pre-assigned instant in time. Since the dynamic
L48@P0: assignment is usually based on some a priori assumptions

L50@P0: the Centre for Ships and Ocean Structures at NTNU.
L51@P0: of the actual system capabilities to ensure its feasibility, it
L52@P0: must be manually reparametrized if something should occur
L53@P0: that would render the actual system incapable of satisfying
L54@P0: it. And if no such tedious reparametrization is performed,
L55@P0: the path particle is essentially left to propagate on its own,
L56@P0: rendering the path system oblivious to the status of the actual
L57@P0: system. As such, the TT scheme represents a feedforward,
L58@P0: open loop type of solution at the path system-actual system
L59@P0: interaction level.
L60@P0: The PF strategy, on the other hand, involves the separate construction of the geometric path and the dynamic
L61@P0: assignment; emphasizing spatial localization as a primary
L62@P0: task objective, while considering the dynamic aspect to be of
L63@P0: secondary importance, sacrificable if necessary. This clearly
L64@P0: represents a more flexible and robust alternative than the TT
L65@P0: scheme. Specifically, this paper treats a PF concept where
L66@P0: the dynamic assignment is associated with the actual particle,
L67@P0: and where the path particle is designed to evolve according
L68@P0: to the actual particle. Thus, the path particle can never leave
L69@P0: the actual particle behind. This entails a closed loop type
L70@P0: of solution to the problem at hand, with the path system
L71@P0: adjusting itself to the actual system. This type of scheme
L72@P0: requires that guidance laws are applied to guide the actual
L73@P0: particle towards the geometric path, stemming from the fact
L74@P0: that the path system now lacks a self-propelled attractor as in
L75@P0: TT. Consequently, the term guidance-based path following
L76@P0: is chosen to describe the concept. The guidance laws should
L77@P0: also ensure that the convergence behaviour of the actual
L78@P0: particle towards the path becomes elegant and natural, which
L79@P0: is usually not the case when applying a traditional TT
L80@P0: scheme. This is especially relevant for mechanical vehicle
L81@P0: systems.
L82@P0: A. Previous Work
L83@P0: Pioneering work on the type of path following scheme under consideration can be found in a paper by Claude Samson
L84@P0: [1], where the author considers path following for wheeled
L85@P0: mobile robots. Omitting a dynamic model, the treatment
L86@P0: is of a purely kinematic nature, making it comparable to
L87@P0: the results of this paper. However, due to Samson’s choice
L88@P0: of the path particle as the exact projection of the actual

L95@P1: are only local. Also, Barbalat’s lemma has to be applied in
L96@P1: the stability analysis due to the way in which the guidance
L97@P1: laws are chosen, entailing that only a convergence result can
L98@P1: be concluded. However, the paper has served as an invaluable
L99@P1: reference and guideline for most of the following work on
L100@P1: the subject.
L101@P1: The initial inspiration for the work reported here can be
L102@P1: traced back to three papers; namely those of Rysdyk [2],
L103@P1: Pettersen and Lefeber [3], and Lapierre et al. [4]. They all essentially treat the problem of guidance-based path following,
L104@P1: although the approaches could seem somewhat different at
L105@P1: first sight. All consider the control of specific actual systems
L106@P1: with distinctive dynamics, and as such intermix the core
L107@P1: concepts of the guidance-based path following scheme with
L108@P1: the control design. While [2] treats unmanned aerial vehicles
L109@P1: (UAVs), [3] treats marine surface vessels (MSVs), and [4]
L110@P1: treats autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs). Relevant
L111@P1: applications can also be found in Do and Pan [5], Encarnação
L112@P1: and Pascoal [6], and del Río et al. [7].
L113@P1: B. Main Contribution
L114@P1: The main contribution of this paper is to develop a
L115@P1: theoretical framework for the concept of guidance-based path
L116@P1: following, which renders all regularly parametrized paths
L117@P1: feasible. By extracting and extending the core concepts of
L118@P1: application-specific cases, the essence is lifted out of any
L119@P1: particular dynamic setting and onto an ideal level, to be
L120@P1: able to state and analyse it properly. Hence, the resulting
L121@P1: theory becomes generally valid. For the sake of intuition and
L122@P1: page limitation, the paper only considers the planar 2D case
L123@P1: and the spatial 3D case. The concept is nevertheless readily
L124@P1: extendable to n-dimensional systems, and will be followed up
L125@P1: with a more in-depth consideration in a separate publication.
L126@P1: II. PROBLEM STATEMENT
L127@P1: The primary objective in guidance-based path following is
L128@P1: to ensure that the actual particle converges to and follows the
L129@P1: desired geometric path, without any temporal requirements.
L130@P1: The secondary objective is to ensure that the actual particle
L131@P1: complies with a desired dynamic behaviour. By then using
L132@P1: the convenient task classification scheme of Skjetne [8], the
L133@P1: guidance-based path following problem can be expressed by
L134@P1: the following two task objectives:
L135@P1: Geometric Task: Make the position of the actual particle
L136@P1: converge to and follow a desired geometric path.
L137@P1: Dynamic Task: Make the speed of the actual particle
L138@P1: converge to and track a desired speed assignment.
L139@P1: The geometric task implies that the actual particle must
L140@P1: move at non-zero speed towards the path particle associated
L141@P1: with the desired geometric path, and that the path particle
L142@P1: in some sense also must move towards the actual particle
L143@P1: despite being restricted to its path. The dynamic task then
